```{r}
covid_end   <- yearmonth("2022 Mar")   # end of the national state of disaster
shock_month <- yearmonth("2020 Apr")   # first full month of hard lockdown
test_start  <- yearmonth("2024 Jul")   # last 24 months held out

# Helpers for inline text -----------------------------------------------
fmt  <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
pfmt <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
month_num <- function(m) year(as.Date(m)) * 12 + month(as.Date(m))
```

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Executive summary

**Title:** Time series regression and exponential smoothing for South African accommodation demand

**Section and topic:** Section 2. Time series regression (trend, seasonal dummies and Fourier terms, intervention variables, regression with ARIMA errors) and exponential smoothing (simple, Holt, damped trend, Holt–Winters and the ETS framework).

**Type of project:** Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. I code the additive Holt–Winters method from first principles (the recursions and the least squares estimation) and check it against `ETS()` in `fable`. The project uses the same series and the same test set as Project 1, so the results of the two projects can be compared directly.

**Question:** How well do the two main Section 2 forecasting approaches, time series regression and exponential smoothing, forecast monthly accommodation demand, and how should each of them deal with the COVID-19 collapse? Can either of them beat the Project 1 SARIMA model?

**Data:** Real-world, publicly available data. Statistics South Africa, *Tourist Accommodation* release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry), January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in @sec-data-source.

**Methods:** *Regression:* a static regression with trend, seasonal dummies and COVID intervention terms, then a regression with ARIMA errors in which the intervention decay rate is chosen by profile likelihood, the seasonal form (dummies or Fourier terms) by AICc and the error model by the Box and Jenkins steps. *Exponential smoothing:* ETS on the raw training data, then the full family of exponential smoothing methods on a series in which the COVID window is replaced by regression-based imputed values, with my own Holt–Winters code as a check, and, as a further check, the same models fitted to the post-COVID years only. All models are diagnosed (Ljung and Box) and compared with the seasonal naive benchmark and the Project 1 SARIMA on the July 2024 to June 2026 test set and by rolling-origin cross-validation.

**Key findings:** A static regression fits the training data closely (adjusted $R^2$ = 0.965), but its errors are strongly autocorrelated, so its standard errors and intervals cannot be trusted. Letting the errors follow an ARIMA(2,1,1) process fixes this and describes the COVID shock with five parameters (a decaying shock with a half-life of about 2.5 months, two pulses and a level shift), giving a test RMSE of 98.8 against 101.6 for the Project 1 SARIMA. Exponential smoothing breaks on the raw data, where the level smoothing parameter goes to 1, but works once the COVID window is imputed: the damped Holt–Winters model was the most accurate model on the test set (RMSE 72.5), while the Project 1 SARIMA remained the best in rolling-origin cross-validation. Details are in @sec-findings.

**What I would do differently:** Add noise to the imputed COVID values (multiple imputation) so that the exponential smoothing models do not treat them as exact, and estimate the intervention decay rate jointly with the other regression parameters rather than on a grid.

**Detailed analysis:** the sections below.
:::

# Introduction and research question

Project 1 modelled monthly nights sold with ARIMA and SARIMA models and found that the COVID-19 collapse in April 2020 was the main obstacle: keeping the COVID months broke the SARIMA model, while treating them as missing worked well. This project turns to the two other forecasting approaches from Section 2.

* **Time series regression** explains the series with explanatory variables: a trend, the calendar month and variables that describe the COVID shock. The COVID months are *used* rather than deleted, because the shock becomes part of the model. The main danger is that a regression assumes independent errors, which time series errors almost never are.
* **Exponential smoothing** forecasts with weighted averages of past observations, with weights that decay exponentially into the past. The methods differ in which components (level, trend, season) they track. Exponential smoothing cannot skip missing values, so the COVID months must be dealt with before fitting.

**Research question.** *How accurately do time series regression and exponential smoothing forecast monthly nights sold, how should each handle the COVID-19 shock, and does either approach beat the Project 1 SARIMA on the same test set?*

## Reading the data

The accommodation series is read exactly as in Project 1.

```{r}
#| label: load-data

raw <- read_excel(tourism_file)

nights_sold <- raw |>
  filter(H03 == "B64100") |>
  select(starts_with("MO")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "code", values_to = "nights") |>
  mutate(Month  = yearmonth(make_date(as.integer(substr(code, 5, 8)),
                                      as.integer(substr(code, 3, 4)), 1L)),
         nights = as.numeric(nights)) |>
  filter(!is.na(nights)) |>
  select(Month, nights) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter_index("2015 Jan" ~ .) |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    Month <  covid_start ~ "Pre-COVID",
    Month <= covid_end   ~ "COVID window",
    TRUE                 ~ "Post-COVID"
  ))

stopifnot(!has_gaps(nights_sold)$.gaps)   # no missing months in the index
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-data
#| fig-cap: "Monthly stay unit nights sold (thousands), January 2015 to June 2026, with the COVID window shaded."
#| fig-height: 3.5

nights_sold |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month), nights)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date(covid_start), xmax = as.Date(covid_end),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")
```

The full exploratory analysis of the accommodation series is in Project 1 and is not repeated here. The points that matter for this project are: the seasonal shape is very stable from year to year, so seasonality can be represented by fixed monthly effects; a log transformation stabilises the size of the seasonal swings; the April 2020 collapse was followed by a recovery that took about two years; and the post-COVID level is still below the pre-COVID level (@fig-data).

## Training and test sets

```{r}
#| label: split

train <- nights_sold |> filter(Month < test_start)
test  <- nights_sold |> filter(Month >= test_start)
```

The training and test sets are identical to Project 1: training from January 2015 to June 2024 (`r nrow(train)` months) and testing from July 2024 to June 2026 (`r nrow(test)` months). Using the same split is what allows the results to be compared across projects.

# Part A: Time series regression

## Describing the COVID shock with intervention variables

A regression can absorb the shock if it is given explanatory variables whose shape matches how the event unfolded. This follows the transfer function idea from the notes. With $t_0$ = April 2020 and everything on the log scale:

* **Decaying shock:** $D_t(\delta) = \delta^{\,t - t_0}$ for $t \ge t_0$ and 0 before. Its coefficient $\omega$ is the immediate effect in April 2020, which then dies out geometrically at rate $\delta$. This is the transfer function $\omega / (1 - \delta L)$ applied to a pulse at $t_0$.
* **Pulses** for March 2020 (lockdown started on 27 March, so the month was only partly affected) and May 2020 (the industry stayed almost completely closed, so the bottom of the collapse lasted two months rather than one).
* **Level shift:** $S_t = 1$ for $t \ge t_0$, allowing a permanent difference between the pre-COVID and post-COVID levels.

```{r}
#| label: covid-vars

covid_vars <- function(df, delta) {
  k0 <- month_num(shock_month)
  df |>
    mutate(k     = month_num(Month) - k0,
           decay = if_else(k >= 0, delta^pmax(k, 0), 0),
           mar20 = as.numeric(k == -1),
           may20 = as.numeric(k == 1),
           step  = as.numeric(k >= 0))
}
```

## Model A1: static regression

The simplest time series regression (fpp3 Chapter 7) has a linear trend, 11 seasonal dummies and the intervention variables, with independent errors:

$$
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).
$$

$\delta$ is fixed at a provisional value of 0.80 here; it is chosen properly in @sec-profile.

```{r}
#| label: fit-static

train_static <- covid_vars(train, 0.80)
test_static  <- covid_vars(test, 0.80)

fit_static <- train_static |>
  model(TSLM(log(nights) ~ trend() + season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step))

static_glance <- glance(fit_static)
static_res    <- augment(fit_static)$.innov
dw_static     <- sum(diff(static_res)^2) / sum(static_res^2)          # Durbin-Watson
lb_static     <- Box.test(static_res, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
r1_static     <- acf(static_res, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-static-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the static regression (Model A1)."
#| fig-height: 5

fit_static |> gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)
```

The fit looks impressive: the adjusted $R^2$ is `r fmt(static_glance$adj_r_squared, 3)`. The residuals tell a different story (@fig-static-resid). They drift in long runs above and below zero, the lag 1 autocorrelation is `r fmt(r1_static, 2)`, the Durbin–Watson statistic is `r fmt(dw_static, 2)` (far below the value of 2 expected for independent errors) and the Ljung and Box test on 24 lags gives p `r pfmt(lb_static)`.

This matters for more than tidiness. With positively autocorrelated errors, the least squares estimates are still unbiased but no longer efficient, the reported standard errors are too small, so the intervention terms look more significant than they are, and the prediction intervals are too narrow. The static regression also ignores useful information: if this month was above the fitted line, next month probably will be too. The remedy, following fpp3 Chapter 10, is to let the error follow an ARIMA process.

## Model A2: regression with ARIMA errors

The dynamic regression replaces the independent error by an ARIMA process:

$$
\log y_t = \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \eta_t, \qquad (1 - L)\,\phi(L)\,\eta_t = \theta(L)\,\varepsilon_t .
$$

Two choices from the static model are revisited. First, the deterministic trend is dropped in favour of a first difference in the errors: after the shock the level does not follow a straight line, and a wandering (stochastic) level is more realistic. With $d = 1$ the intercept and trend are differenced away, which is why they do not appear. Second, the seasonality is kept *deterministic* (dummies) rather than handled with a seasonal difference. In Project 1, the airline model fitted with the COVID months included estimated a seasonal MA coefficient of -1.000. A seasonal MA factor $(1 - L^{12})$ that cancels the seasonal difference is the classic sign that the seasonal pattern is fixed rather than evolving, so that seasonal differencing is over-differencing. The seasonal plots in Project 1 point the same way, and the exponential smoothing models below confirm it independently: every seasonal ETS model puts the seasonal smoothing parameter $\gamma$ at or near its lower bound, so the seasonal pattern barely changes over ten years.

### Choosing the decay rate by profile likelihood {#sec-profile}

The decay rate $\delta$ enters the model non-linearly, so it cannot be estimated by `ARIMA()` directly. Instead I profile it: for each $\delta$ on a grid from 0.70 to 0.96, the model is fitted (with the ARIMA error orders chosen by AICc) and the AICc recorded. The value of $\delta$ with the smallest AICc is used. Because $\delta$ is estimated, the model really has one more parameter than `ARIMA()` reports; this does not change the ranking along the grid.

```{r}
#| label: profile-delta

delta_grid <- seq(0.70, 0.96, by = 0.02)

profile <- bind_rows(lapply(delta_grid, function(dl) {
  f <- covid_vars(train, dl) |>
    model(reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                        pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)))
  tibble(delta = dl,
         AICc  = glance(f)$AICc,
         spec  = format(f$reg[[1]]))
}))

delta_hat <- profile$delta[which.min(profile$AICc)]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile
#| fig-cap: "Profile of AICc against the decay rate. The selected value is marked in red."
#| fig-height: 3

ggplot(profile, aes(delta, AICc)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = filter(profile, delta == delta_hat), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(delta), y = "AICc")
```

The AICc is minimised at $\hat\delta$ = `r fmt(delta_hat, 2)` (@fig-profile). A decay rate of `r fmt(delta_hat, 2)` means that the temporary part of the shock halves every `r fmt(log(0.5) / log(delta_hat), 1)` months and has fallen to `r pct(delta_hat^12)` of its initial size after a year. `r if (delta_hat <= min(delta_grid) + 1e-8) "The minimum is at the edge of the grid, so a smaller value cannot be ruled out." else ""`

### Seasonal dummies or Fourier terms?

Fourier terms ($\sin(2\pi k t/12)$ and $\cos(2\pi k t/12)$ for $k = 1, \dots, K$) are the other standard way to put seasonality into a regression. With small $K$ they describe a smooth seasonal shape with fewer parameters; with $K = 6$ they are equivalent to the 11 dummies. I compare the two at $\hat\delta$ by AICc. All the models have the same response and the same order of differencing, so their AICc values are comparable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fourier
#| tbl-cap: "AICc of the regression with ARIMA errors for different representations of the seasonal pattern (decay rate fixed at its profile estimate). The ARIMA error orders are chosen by AICc for each row."

train_reg <- covid_vars(train, delta_hat)
test_reg  <- covid_vars(test, delta_hat)

seas_forms <- c("Seasonal dummies" = "season()",
                "Fourier, K = 1"   = "fourier(K = 1)",
                "Fourier, K = 2"   = "fourier(K = 2)",
                "Fourier, K = 3"   = "fourier(K = 3)",
                "Fourier, K = 4"   = "fourier(K = 4)",
                "Fourier, K = 5"   = "fourier(K = 5)")

seas_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(seas_forms), function(nm) {
  f <- as.formula(paste("log(nights) ~", seas_forms[[nm]],
                        "+ decay + mar20 + may20 + step + pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)"))
  m <- train_reg |> model(r = ARIMA(!!f))
  tibble(`Seasonal terms` = nm,
         `Seasonal parameters` = c(11, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10)[match(nm, names(seas_forms))],
         `Error model` = format(m$r[[1]]),
         AICc = glance(m)$AICc)
}))

seas_tbl |> kable(digits = 1)

best_seas <- seas_tbl$`Seasonal terms`[which.min(seas_tbl$AICc)]
```

The lowest AICc belongs to the model with **`r tolower(best_seas)`**. `r if (best_seas == "Seasonal dummies") "The low-order Fourier models are clearly worse: the accommodation seasonal pattern has a sharp December peak, a smaller Easter and mid-year bump and a dip in winter, which needs many harmonics to describe. Fourier terms pay off mainly for long seasonal periods (weekly data with period 52, or daily data), where dummies would need many more parameters. Seasonal dummies are used from here on." else "A smooth seasonal shape is enough here, which saves parameters. Note, however, that the final model below uses seasonal dummies for comparability with Project 1."`

### Fitting the model (Box and Jenkins loop)

```{r}
#| label: fit-reg

# Steps 3 and 4: residuals from the regression part, before choosing the ARIMA errors
ols <- train_reg |>
  model(TSLM(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step))
ols_resid <- augment(ols)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ols-resid
#| fig-cap: "Steps 3 and 4 of the modelling procedure for the error process: first differences of the residuals from the regression part, with their ACF and PACF."

ols_resid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(.resid), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)
```

Following the seven-step modelling procedure used in Projects 1 and 2, the regression residuals are examined before choosing the error model. Without the trend the residuals from the regression part wander, so a first difference is taken. @fig-ols-resid shows the differenced residuals with their ACF and PACF, which point to a low order ARMA structure with no seasonal spikes left (the dummies have removed the seasonality). The orders are then chosen by AICc, and the model is estimated by maximum likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: fit-reg-final

fit_reg <- train_reg |>
  model(
    Reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                  pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))
  )

reg_spec <- format(fit_reg$Reg[[1]])
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reg-coef
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated intervention coefficients (log scale) of the regression with ARIMA errors. Seasonal dummy and ARMA coefficients are omitted for space."

reg_coef <- tidy(fit_reg) |>
  filter(term %in% c("decay", "mar20", "may20", "step"))

reg_coef |>
  select(Term = term, Estimate = estimate,
         `Std. error` = std.error, `p-value` = p.value) |>
  kable(digits = 3)

rc <- function(m, t, col = "estimate") reg_coef[[col]][reg_coef$.model == m & reg_coef$term == t]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-intervention
#| fig-cap: "Contribution of the intervention terms (decay, pulses and level shift combined) in the regression with ARIMA errors, expressed as a percentage reduction in demand. The later recovery is carried by the ARIMA error and is not shown."
#| fig-height: 3.2

effect <- train_reg |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(log_effect = rc("Reg", "decay") * decay + rc("Reg", "mar20") * mar20 +
           rc("Reg", "may20") * may20 + rc("Reg", "step") * step,
         lost = 1 - exp(log_effect)) |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("2019 Jul"))

ggplot(effect, aes(as.Date(Month), 100 * lost)) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reduction from intervention terms (%)")
```

The selected error model is `r reg_spec`. The estimates have a direct interpretation on the log scale. The decaying shock has $\hat\omega$ = `r fmt(rc("Reg", "decay"), 2)`; combined with the May 2020 pulse and the level shift, this reproduces a loss of almost all demand in April and May 2020. The level shift is $\hat\lambda$ = `r fmt(rc("Reg", "step"), 3)` (p `r pfmt(rc("Reg", "step", "p.value"))`). This needs careful interpretation. Because the error $\eta_t$ has a unit root, it has its own wandering level, and the slow two-year recovery is carried by the error rather than by the intervention terms: the decaying shock dies out quickly (see the half-life above), and $\hat\lambda$ is the part of the April 2020 drop that did *not* decay geometrically. It is therefore not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels; that gap is estimated directly in @sec-impute. @fig-intervention shows the contribution of the intervention terms alone, which is why it stays flat after 2020; the recovery towards the post-COVID level happens in the error process. The standard errors are now valid only because the errors are modelled; compare the static regression, whose standard errors were too small.

### Residual diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: reg-diag

reg_aug <- augment(fit_reg)

n_arma <- tidy(fit_reg) |>
  filter(grepl("^(ar|ma)[0-9]+$", term)) |>
  count(.model, name = "dof")

reg_lb <- reg_aug |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(n_arma, by = ".model") |>
  mutate(dof = coalesce(dof, 0L)) |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(lb_p = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box",
                            fitdf = first(dof))$p.value,
            .groups = "drop")

lbp <- function(m) reg_lb$lb_p[reg_lb$.model == m]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the regression with ARIMA errors."
#| fig-height: 5

fit_reg |> select(Reg) |> gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)
```

The Ljung and Box test on 24 lags (degrees of freedom reduced by the number of ARMA coefficients) gives p = `r pfmt(lbp("Reg"))`. `r if (lbp("Reg") > 0.05) "The innovations of the regression model are consistent with white noise and show no remaining seasonal structure, so the deterministic seasonal dummies are adequate. Compared with the static regression, the long runs in the residuals have disappeared: the ARIMA error has absorbed the autocorrelation. The model passes the residual check (step 6) and can be used to forecast." else "Some autocorrelation remains in the innovations of the regression model, so by the Box and Jenkins rule it should not be used for forecasting without revisiting the error orders."`

# Part B: Exponential smoothing

## Model B1: ETS on the raw training data

The `ETS()` function selects the error, trend and seasonal forms (additive, multiplicative or none) by AICc and estimates the smoothing parameters and initial states by maximum likelihood. Exponential smoothing cannot skip missing observations, so the first attempt simply fits ETS to the training data *including* the COVID months, on both the original and the log scale.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ets-raw

fit_ets_raw <- train |>
  model(`ETS raw (original scale)` = ETS(nights),
        `ETS raw (log scale)`      = ETS(log(nights)))

ets_par_tbl <- function(fit) {
  tidy(fit) |>
    filter(term %in% c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "phi")) |>
    select(.model, term, estimate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate) |>
    left_join(tibble(.model = names(fit),
                     Form = vapply(names(fit), function(m) format(fit[[m]][[1]]), "")),
              by = ".model") |>
    relocate(Form, .after = .model)
}

raw_tbl <- ets_par_tbl(fit_ets_raw)
alpha_raw <- raw_tbl$alpha
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ets-raw
#| tbl-cap: "ETS models selected by AICc on the raw training data (COVID months included)."

raw_tbl |> rename(Model = .model) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

This is the exponential smoothing version of the problem Project 1 had with SARIMA. On both scales the level smoothing parameter is at its upper limit ($\hat\alpha \approx$ `r fmt(max(alpha_raw), 3)`): the only way the method can follow a collapse of more than 95% and a two-year recovery is to reset the level to the latest observation every month. `r if (raw_tbl$Form[2] == "<ETS(A,N,N)>" || grepl("N,N", raw_tbl$Form[2])) "On the log scale the selected model even has *no seasonal component*: on the log scale the April 2020 drop is many times larger than the seasonal swings, so the likelihood gains nothing from tracking the season. A model with no seasonality for a series this seasonal is clearly wrong." else ""` With $\alpha = 1$ the forecasts are simply the last observation (plus the seasonal pattern, if there is one), the residual variance is inflated by the COVID months and the prediction intervals are very wide. The COVID window has to be dealt with before exponential smoothing can work.

## Imputing the COVID window with a regression {#sec-impute}

Three ways of handling the window are possible: (1) fit only to the post-COVID months, which leaves just over two years of data to estimate 12 seasonal effects (tested as a check in @sec-post); (2) remove the estimated intervention effect from Part A; or (3) replace the COVID months by values that describe what demand would have looked like without the pandemic. Option (2) does not help much: the regression explains the shock partly through its ARIMA error, so the "adjusted" series still contains most of the recovery dynamics. I therefore use option (3), with a regression as the imputation model.

The imputation regression is fitted only to the **non-COVID** months:

$$
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \lambda R_t + \varepsilon_t,
$$

where $R_t$ is a ramp: 0 before March 2020, 1 after March 2022, and rising linearly through the window. Since $R_t$ only takes the values 0 and 1 in the months used for fitting, $\lambda$ is the difference between the pre- and post-COVID levels; inside the window the ramp produces a straight-line transition between the two levels, with the usual seasonal pattern on top. The fitted values in the window are used as the imputed values.

```{r}
#| label: impute

impute_covid <- function(df) {
  n_win <- month_num(covid_end) - month_num(covid_start) + 2
  df <- df |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(t      = row_number(),
           mon    = factor(month(as.Date(Month))),
           in_win = Month >= covid_start & Month <= covid_end,
           ramp   = pmin(pmax((month_num(Month) - month_num(covid_start) + 1) / n_win, 0), 1),
           y_obs  = if_else(in_win, NA_real_, log(nights)))
  fit <- lm(y_obs ~ t + mon + ramp, data = df)   # lm drops the NA months
  df |>
    mutate(log_fit     = predict(fit, newdata = df),
           nights_imp  = if_else(in_win, exp(log_fit), nights)) |>
    select(-t, -mon, -y_obs, -log_fit) |>
    structure(imputation_fit = fit)          # keep the fitted model for reporting
}

train_imp_tbl <- impute_covid(train)
imp_lm        <- attr(train_imp_tbl, "imputation_fit")
train_imp     <- train_imp_tbl |> as_tsibble(index = Month)

imp_r2   <- summary(imp_lm)$r.squared
imp_ramp <- coef(imp_lm)[["ramp"]]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-impute
#| fig-cap: "Training data on the original scale (grey) and the series used for exponential smoothing, in which the COVID window (shaded) is replaced by the regression-imputed values (red)."
#| fig-height: 3.5

train_imp |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date(covid_start), xmax = as.Date(covid_end),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights_imp), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")
```

The imputation regression explains `r pct(imp_r2, 1)` of the variation in the non-COVID months, and the estimated difference between the post- and pre-COVID levels is `r fmt(imp_ramp, 3)` on the log scale (`r pct(exp(imp_ramp) - 1, 1)`). This is the clearest estimate in the project of how far demand remains below its pre-COVID path. It is much smaller than the level shift in the regression with ARIMA errors ($\hat\lambda$ = `r fmt(rc("Reg", "step"), 3)`), which confirms the point made there: in that model the error process carries part of the recovery, so $\hat\lambda$ is not the long-run gap. The imputed values (@fig-impute) carry the seasonal pattern smoothly across the gap. Their weakness is that they contain no noise, which I return to in the discussion.

## Model B2: Holt–Winters from first principles

To make sure I understand what `ETS()` is doing, I implement the additive Holt–Winters method myself (fpp3 Section 8.3). With $y_t$ the log of the imputed series, $\ell_t$ the level, $b_t$ the trend and $s_t$ the seasonal effect, the one-step forecast and the error are

$$
\hat y_{t \mid t-1} = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + s_{t-12}, \qquad e_t = y_t - \hat y_{t \mid t-1},
$$

and the components are updated in error-correction form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t, \\
b_t    &= b_{t-1} + \beta e_t, \\
s_t    &= s_{t-12} + \gamma e_t .
\end{aligned}
$$

Each update moves a component in the direction of the latest error, and the smoothing parameters say how far. The $h$-step forecast is $\hat y_{T+h \mid T} = \ell_T + h\, b_T + s_{T+h-12k}$, where $k$ makes the seasonal index refer to the last observed year. With additive errors, maximising the Gaussian likelihood is the same as minimising the sum of squared one-step errors (the error variance can be profiled out), so I estimate the three smoothing parameters and the 13 free initial states ($\ell_0$, $b_0$ and 11 seasonal effects; the 12th is set so the seasonal effects sum to zero) by minimising the SSE with `optim()`. The parameter bounds match those in `fable` (between 0.0001 and 0.9999).

```{r}
#| label: own-hw

# Additive Holt-Winters filter -------------------------------------------
# par = (alpha, beta, gamma, l0, b0, s_{-11}, ..., s_{-1});
# the last seasonal state s_0 makes the 12 initial effects sum to zero.
hw_filter <- function(par, y, m = 12) {
  alpha <- par[1]; beta <- par[2]; gamma <- par[3]
  level <- par[4]; trend <- par[5]
  s     <- c(par[6:(4 + m)], -sum(par[6:(4 + m)]))  # s[1] is the effect for the next month
  n <- length(y); e <- yhat <- numeric(n)
  for (t in 1:n) {
    yhat[t] <- level + trend + s[1]
    e[t]    <- y[t] - yhat[t]
    new_level <- level + trend + alpha * e[t]
    trend     <- trend + beta * e[t]
    s         <- c(s[-1], s[1] + gamma * e[t])        # rotate the seasonal states
    level     <- new_level
  }
  list(e = e, fitted = yhat, level = level, trend = trend, season = s)
}

hw_forecast <- function(state, h, m = 12) {
  state$level + (1:h) * state$trend + rep(state$season, length.out = h)
}

# Estimation by least squares --------------------------------------------
y_imp <- log(train_imp$nights_imp)
sse   <- function(par) sum(hw_filter(par, y_imp)$e^2)

# Starting values: classical decomposition of the first two years
first2 <- y_imp[1:24]
s_init <- y_imp[1:12] - mean(y_imp[1:12])
start  <- c(0.3, 0.01, 0.1,
            mean(first2[1:12]), (mean(first2[13:24]) - mean(first2[1:12])) / 12,
            (s_init - mean(s_init))[1:11])

own_opt <- optim(start, sse, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(rep(1e-4, 3), rep(-Inf, 13)),
                 upper = c(rep(0.9999, 3), rep(Inf, 13)),
                 control = list(maxit = 10000))
own_hw  <- hw_filter(own_opt$par, y_imp)

# The same model in fable --------------------------------------------------
fit_hw_fable <- train_imp |>
  model(HW = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A")))
fable_par <- tidy(fit_hw_fable)
fable_sse <- sum(augment(fit_hw_fable)$.innov^2)
fp <- function(t) fable_par$estimate[fable_par$term == t]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-own-hw
#| tbl-cap: "My Holt-Winters implementation against ETS(A,A,A) from fable, fitted to the same log imputed series."

tibble(
  Quantity = c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "Initial level", "Initial trend",
               "SSE", "Optimiser converged"),
  `Own code` = c(fmt(own_opt$par[1:3], 4), fmt(own_opt$par[4], 3),
                 fmt(own_opt$par[5], 5), fmt(own_opt$value, 5),
                 ifelse(own_opt$convergence == 0, "Yes", "No")),
  `fable ETS(A,A,A)` = c(fmt(c(fp("alpha"), fp("beta"), fp("gamma")), 4),
                         fmt(fp("l[0]"), 3), fmt(fp("b[0]"), 5),
                         fmt(fable_sse, 5), "")
) |> kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: hw-check
#| include: false
own_fc   <- hw_forecast(own_hw, 24)
fable_fc <- forecast(fit_hw_fable, h = 24) |> pull(.mean)   # back-transformed mean
own_vs_fable_fc <- max(abs(exp(own_fc) - fable_fc) / fable_fc)
```

The two fits agree closely (@tbl-own-hw). `r if (own_opt$value <= fable_sse) paste0("My optimiser actually reaches a slightly *lower* SSE (", fmt(own_opt$value, 5), " against ", fmt(fable_sse, 5), "), so the small differences in the parameters come from the two optimisers stopping at different points on a very flat surface, not from a difference in the model.") else paste0("The SSE from fable is slightly lower (", fmt(fable_sse, 5), " against ", fmt(own_opt$value, 5), "), so my optimiser stopped a little short of the minimum on a flat surface.")` Both put $\beta$ and $\gamma$ at the lower bound, which means the trend and the seasonal pattern are essentially fixed at their initial values, while the level adapts with $\hat\alpha \approx$ `r fmt(own_opt$par[1], 2)`. This matches the finding from Project 1 that the seasonal pattern is very stable. The 24-month forecasts from the two implementations differ by at most `r pct(own_vs_fable_fc, 1)` (part of this is that fable's forecast is the bias-adjusted mean, while mine is the back-transformed median). Writing the recursions out also made something clear that is easy to miss when calling `ETS()`: the initial states are parameters too, and with 13 of them against three smoothing parameters they dominate the estimation.

## Model B3: the exponential smoothing family on the imputed series

With the window imputed, the full family from fpp3 Chapter 8 can be fitted to the log series. AICc can be used to compare these models because they all have the same response and none of them is differenced.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ets-family

fit_ets <- train_imp |>
  model(
    SES                 = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("N")),
    Holt                = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("N")),
    `Damped Holt`       = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("N")),
    `ETS(A,N,A)`        = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters`      = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`         = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A")),
    `ETS auto`          = ETS(log(nights_imp))
  )

ets_lb <- augment(fit_ets) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(lb_p = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value, .groups = "drop")

ets_tbl <- ets_par_tbl(fit_ets) |>
  left_join(glance(fit_ets) |> select(.model, AICc), by = ".model") |>
  left_join(ets_lb, by = ".model") |>
  mutate(.model = factor(.model, levels = names(fit_ets))) |>
  arrange(.model)

auto_form <- ets_tbl$Form[ets_tbl$.model == "ETS auto"]
best_aicc <- as.character(ets_tbl$.model[which.min(ets_tbl$AICc)])
elb <- function(m) ets_tbl$lb_p[ets_tbl$.model == m]
ep  <- function(m, col) ets_tbl[[col]][ets_tbl$.model == m]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ets-family
#| tbl-cap: "Exponential smoothing models fitted to the log imputed series: estimated smoothing parameters, AICc and the Ljung and Box p-value on 24 lags of the innovations."

ets_tbl |>
  mutate(lb_p = pfmt(lb_p)) |>
  rename(Model = .model, `Ljung-Box p` = lb_p) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 3, 4, 3, 4, 1, 0))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ets-components
#| fig-cap: "Components of the damped Holt-Winters model on the log scale: level, slope and seasonal effects."
#| fig-height: 5

fit_ets |> select(`Damped HW`) |> components() |> autoplot() + labs(x = NULL)
```

The results sort the models into two groups (@tbl-ets-family). The non-seasonal methods (SES, Holt, damped Holt) have far higher AICc values and their innovations are strongly autocorrelated (Ljung and Box p `r pfmt(max(elb("SES"), elb("Holt"), elb("Damped Holt")))`), because they leave the whole seasonal pattern in the errors. They fail the residual check (step 6) immediately. The seasonal models all pass the white noise check, and the automatic selection chooses `r auto_form`.

The seasonal models differ mainly in what they do with the trend:

* `ETS(A,N,A)` has no trend: forecasts are flat apart from the season. Its AICc is `r fmt(ep("ETS(A,N,A)", "AICc"))`.
* `Holt-Winters` has an additive trend with $\hat\beta$ at the lower bound, so the slope is fixed at its initial value. The forecasts extrapolate that slope linearly for the full 24 months. AICc `r fmt(ep("Holt-Winters", "AICc"))`.
* `Damped HW` multiplies the slope by $\phi$ = `r fmt(ep("Damped HW", "phi"), 3)` each month, so its effect fades and the long-run forecast levels off. AICc `r fmt(ep("Damped HW", "AICc"))`.

The AICc differences between the three seasonal models are `r if (diff(range(ets_tbl$AICc[ets_tbl$.model %in% c("ETS(A,N,A)", "Holt-Winters", "Damped HW")])) < 4) "small (less than 4), so the training data alone cannot separate them clearly" else "large enough to prefer the lowest AICc model"`. The choice matters much more for long horizons than for one-step fit, so the test set below is the real arbiter. My prior expectation, from the literature on damped trends (Gardner and McKenzie, 1985), is that a damped trend will forecast better than a linear one over two years.

## Model B4: a check using the post-COVID years only {#sec-post}

The imputation approach keeps all ten years of data but fills the COVID window with values that were never observed. A simpler alternative is to drop everything before April 2022 and fit exponential smoothing only to the post-COVID months. At first sight little should be lost, because exponential smoothing already gives the most weight to the latest observations. That is true for the *level*, but not for the other components here. In the models above, $\gamma$ and $\beta$ sit at or near their lower bounds, so the seasonal pattern and the slope are hardly updated at all: they stay close to their *initial* values, which are estimated from the whole series back to 2015. The early years therefore still shape the seasonal pattern and the trend, however small their weight in the level. Fitting to the post-COVID months only is the one way to let those components reflect current behaviour. The cost is data: April 2022 to June 2024 gives just `r nrow(filter(train, Month >= yearmonth("2022 Apr")))` months to estimate up to four smoothing parameters and 13 initial states.

```{r}
#| label: fit-post

post_start <- yearmonth("2022 Apr")
train_post <- train |> filter(Month >= post_start)
ets_forms  <- c("ETS(A,N,A)", "Holt-Winters", "Damped HW")

fit_post <- train_post |>
  model(
    `ETS(A,N,A)`   = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`    = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))
  )

# Test set forecasts from both versions of each model
fc_ets_tbl <- function(fit, label) {
  forecast(fit, h = 24) |>
    hilo(level = 95) |>
    unpack_hilo(`95%`) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    select(Model = .model, Month, mean = .mean, lo95 = `95%_lower`, hi95 = `95%_upper`) |>
    mutate(Data = label)
}

post_fc <- bind_rows(
  fc_ets_tbl(fit_ets |> select(all_of(ets_forms)), "Imputed series, 2015 to 2024"),
  fc_ets_tbl(fit_post, "Post-COVID only, 2022 to 2024")
) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(test) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  filter(!is.na(mean)) |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = ets_forms))

sn_rmse <- train |>
  model(SNAIVE(nights)) |>
  forecast(h = 24) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(test) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2))) |>
  pull(RMSE)

post_acc <- post_fc |>
  group_by(Model, Data) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - mean)^2)),
            MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - mean) / actual),
            `Cover 95%` = mean(actual >= lo95 & actual <= hi95),
            `Mean 95% width` = mean(hi95 - lo95),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = ets_forms)) |>
  arrange(Model, Data)

post_par <- ets_par_tbl(fit_post) |>
  mutate(.model = factor(.model, levels = ets_forms)) |>
  arrange(.model)

pa  <- function(m, d, col) post_acc[[col]][post_acc$Model == m & post_acc$Data == d]
d_imp  <- "Imputed series, 2015 to 2024"
d_post <- "Post-COVID only, 2022 to 2024"
post_better <- ets_forms[vapply(ets_forms, function(m) isTRUE(pa(m, d_post, "RMSE") < pa(m, d_imp, "RMSE")), logical(1))]
best_post   <- as.character(post_acc$Model[post_acc$Data == d_post][which.min(post_acc$RMSE[post_acc$Data == d_post])])
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-post-par
#| tbl-cap: "Smoothing parameters of the seasonal exponential smoothing models fitted to the post-COVID months only (April 2022 to June 2024, log scale)."

post_par |> rename(Model = .model) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-post-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Test set accuracy (July 2024 to June 2026) of each seasonal exponential smoothing model fitted to the imputed series and to the post-COVID months only. RMSE and mean 95% interval width are in thousands of nights."

post_acc |>
  mutate(`Cover 95%` = pct(`Cover 95%`)) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-post-fc
#| fig-cap: "Test set forecasts and 95% intervals from each model fitted to the imputed series (blue) and to the post-COVID months only (orange). Black: observed values."
#| fig-height: 6.5

ggplot(post_fc, aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo95, ymax = hi95, fill = Data), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean, colour = Data), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = as_tibble(test), aes(x = as.Date(Month), y = nights),
            colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Model), ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue4", "darkorange3")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue4", "darkorange3")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-post-season
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal effects (log scale) at the end of the training period, from the ETS(A,N,A) model fitted to the imputed series and to the post-COVID months only."
#| fig-height: 3.2

season_end <- function(fit, label) {
  components(fit) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    filter(!is.na(season)) |>
    slice_tail(n = 12) |>
    mutate(month = month(as.Date(Month)), Data = label) |>
    select(month, season, Data)
}

seas_cmp <- bind_rows(
  season_end(fit_ets |> select(`ETS(A,N,A)`), d_imp),
  season_end(fit_post |> select(`ETS(A,N,A)`), d_post)
)
seas_gap <- seas_cmp |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Data, values_from = season) |>
  mutate(gap = abs(exp(.data[[d_post]] - .data[[d_imp]]) - 1))

ggplot(seas_cmp, aes(month, season, colour = Data)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue4", "darkorange3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Seasonal effect (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**What happens with less data.** With only `r nrow(train_post)` months, each seasonal effect is effectively estimated from two or three values. Across the three post-COVID fits (@tbl-post-par), the level parameter ranges from $\hat\alpha$ = `r fmt(min(post_par$alpha, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r fmt(max(post_par$alpha, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, and the largest seasonal parameter is $\hat\gamma$ = `r fmt(max(post_par$gamma, na.rm = TRUE), 4)`. `r if (max(post_par$gamma, na.rm = TRUE) < 0.05) "As on the full series, the seasonal pattern is held essentially fixed: two years of data contain no evidence that it is changing." else "Unlike the full series, the seasonal pattern is allowed to change noticeably, which with so few observations is more likely to reflect noise than genuine change."` `r if (diff(range(post_par$alpha, na.rm = TRUE)) > 0.3) "The level parameter, in contrast, differs widely between the three forms, a sign that the short sample cannot pin down how quickly the level should adapt." else ""`

**Forecast accuracy.** On the test set (@tbl-post-acc, @fig-post-fc), the best of the post-COVID fits is **`r best_post`** (RMSE `r fmt(pa(best_post, d_post, "RMSE"))`), against `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_imp, "RMSE"))` for the damped Holt–Winters model on the imputed series and `r fmt(sn_rmse)` for seasonal naive. `r if (length(post_better) == 0) "None of the three models improves when the earlier years are dropped." else if (length(post_better) == length(ets_forms)) "All three models improve when the earlier years are dropped." else paste0("Dropping the earlier years helps ", paste(post_better, collapse = " and "), " but not the other ", ifelse(length(post_better) == 1, "two", "one"), ", so the ranking of the three models changes with the training window.")` The ETS(A,N,A) model moves from an RMSE of `r fmt(pa("ETS(A,N,A)", d_imp, "RMSE"))` to `r fmt(pa("ETS(A,N,A)", d_post, "RMSE"))`, Holt–Winters from `r fmt(pa("Holt-Winters", d_imp, "RMSE"))` to `r fmt(pa("Holt-Winters", d_post, "RMSE"))`, and damped Holt–Winters from `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_imp, "RMSE"))` to `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_post, "RMSE"))`. With two years of data, the trend each model estimates comes from a very short stretch of the recovery, so which model forecasts best depends heavily on how that short-run slope happens to continue.

The large improvement for Holt–Winters shows where the problem with the undamped model on the imputed series lies. There, the slope is fixed at the value estimated for the start of the series in 2015, which is slightly negative, and it is extrapolated for two full years, so the forecasts drift steadily below the data (@fig-post-fc). Fitted to the post-COVID months, the slope comes from the recovery instead, which happened to continue through the test period. But this version is not a better model so much as a different gamble. Its smoothing parameters are all close to zero ($\hat\alpha$ = `r fmt(post_par$alpha[post_par$.model == "Holt-Winters"], 4)`), so it is essentially a fixed straight line plus a fixed seasonal pattern drawn through 27 months. Its 95% intervals are the narrowest of all (mean width `r fmt(pa("Holt-Winters", d_post, "Mean 95% width"), 0)` thousand nights), yet they still miss `r pct(1 - pa("Holt-Winters", d_post, "Cover 95%"))` of the test months.

The damped model is the most revealing result of the check. Fitted to completely different training windows, it gives almost the same forecast accuracy (RMSE `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_imp, "RMSE"))` and `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_post, "RMSE"))`), because damping makes the long-horizon forecast depend much less on exactly how the slope is estimated. That robustness is a stronger argument for the damped trend than its single best test-set score. The short window still has a cost: the damped model's 95% intervals are wider when it is fitted to the post-COVID months only (mean width `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_post, "Mean 95% width"), 0)` against `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_imp, "Mean 95% width"), 0)` thousand nights), reflecting the extra uncertainty in parameters estimated from two years of data.

**Seasonal pattern.** `r if (max(seas_gap$gap) < 0.05) paste0("The seasonal effects learned from the post-COVID months alone are close to those from the full imputed series (@fig-post-season): the largest difference in any month is ", pct(max(seas_gap$gap), 1), ". This confirms, from a different angle, the finding from Project 1 that the seasonal shape survived COVID unchanged, and it means that the long history is not distorting the seasonal pattern. Its value lies in pinning down the level and the trend, which is exactly where the short-window fits are least stable.") else paste0("The seasonal effects learned from the post-COVID months alone differ from those of the full imputed series by up to ", pct(max(seas_gap$gap), 1), " in a single month (@fig-post-season). With only two or three observations behind each month, part of this difference is likely to be noise rather than a genuine change in the seasonal shape, which Project 1 found to be very stable.")`

**Conclusion of the check.** Using only the post-COVID years avoids imputation entirely, and `r if (pa(best_post, d_post, "RMSE") < sn_rmse) "for some model forms it forecasts well" else "yet none of the forms even beats the seasonal naive benchmark"`. But the results are fragile: with so little data the outcome depends on the choice of trend, and there is no way to tell in advance which choice will work. The imputed series gives the models enough history to estimate the seasonal pattern and the trend reliably, which is why it remains the main approach in this project.

# Forecast evaluation

## Forecasts on the test set

All models produce forecasts for July 2024 to June 2026 from the end of June 2024, with 80% and 95% prediction intervals. Two reference models are included: the seasonal naive benchmark and the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)~12~ model from Project 1 with the COVID months treated as missing, refitted here with exactly the same specification. For models fitted on the log scale, point forecasts are back-transformed to the mean (with the bias adjustment), as in Project 1.

```{r}
#| label: forecasts

train_B <- train |>
  mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))

fit_ref <- train_B |>
  model(`SARIMA (Project 1)` = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1)))
fit_sn  <- train |> model(`Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(nights))

# Summarise each forecast table separately (the distributions differ in type)
fc_summ <- function(fc, label = NULL) {
  dcol <- fc[[fabletools::distribution_var(fc)]]
  out <- tibble(.model = fc$.model, Month = fc$Month, mean = fc$.mean,
                lo80 = quantile(dcol, 0.10), hi80 = quantile(dcol, 0.90),
                lo95 = quantile(dcol, 0.025), hi95 = quantile(dcol, 0.975))
  if (!is.null(label)) out$.model <- label
  out
}

fc_all <- bind_rows(
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_sn,  h = 24)),
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_ref, h = 24)),
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_static, new_data = test_static), "Static regression"),
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_reg |> select(Reg), new_data = test_reg)),
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_ets_raw |> select(`ETS raw (original scale)`), h = 24)),
  fc_summ(forecast(fit_ets |> select(SES, `ETS(A,N,A)`, `Holt-Winters`, `Damped HW`), h = 24))
) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(test) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month")
```

```{r}
#| label: accuracy

# MASE scale: in-sample seasonal naive MAE on the training data
mase_scale <- mean(abs(diff(train$nights, lag = 12)))

model_order <- c("Seasonal naive", "SARIMA (Project 1)",
                 "Static regression", "Reg",
                 "ETS raw (original scale)", "SES", "ETS(A,N,A)", "Holt-Winters", "Damped HW")

ets_raw_lb <- augment(fit_ets_raw |> select(`ETS raw (original scale)`)) |>
  as_tibble() |> pull(.innov) |> Box.test(lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box") |> getElement("p.value")

yn <- function(p) if_else(p > 0.05, "Yes", "No")
diag_status <- tibble(
  Model = model_order,
  `Passes diagnostics` = c("Benchmark", "Yes (Project 1)",
                           yn(lb_static), yn(lbp("Reg")),
                           yn(ets_raw_lb), yn(elb("SES")), yn(elb("ETS(A,N,A)")),
                           yn(elb("Holt-Winters")), yn(elb("Damped HW"))))

results <- fc_all |>
  group_by(Model = .model) |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - mean)^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(actual - mean)),
    MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - mean) / actual),
    MASE = mean(abs(actual - mean)) / mase_scale,
    cover80 = mean(actual >= lo80 & actual <= hi80),
    cover95 = mean(actual >= lo95 & actual <= hi95),
    width95 = mean(hi95 - lo95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(diag_status, by = "Model") |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = model_order)) |>
  arrange(Model)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Test set accuracy, July 2024 to June 2026. RMSE, MAE and mean 95% interval width are in thousands of nights. MASE uses the in-sample seasonal naive error as its scale, the same for every model. The last column records whether the model passed the residual diagnostics (Ljung and Box, 24 lags, 5% level)."

results |>
  mutate(cover80 = pct(cover80), cover95 = pct(cover95)) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0),
        col.names = c("Model", "RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE (%)", "MASE",
                      "Cover 80%", "Cover 95%", "Mean 95% width", "Passes diagnostics"),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
candidates <- results |> filter(`Passes diagnostics` %in% c("Yes", "Yes (Project 1)"))
best_cand  <- as.character(candidates$Model[which.min(candidates$RMSE)])
beats_sn   <- function(m) rg(m, "RMSE") < rg("Seasonal naive", "RMSE")
best_ets   <- c("ETS(A,N,A)", "Holt-Winters", "Damped HW")[
```

## Rolling-origin cross-validation

A single 24-month test set gives one realisation of each model's forecast errors, so the ranking could be luck. As in Project 1, I also use an expanding window: the models are refitted at each of 13 origins from June 2024 to June 2025 and forecast 1 to 12 months ahead, and the errors are averaged by horizon. The imputation regression is refitted at every origin. To keep the computation manageable, the regression keeps $\hat\delta$ and its ARIMA error orders fixed at the values chosen above; the ETS forms are also fixed, but all parameters are re-estimated. All the origins fall inside the test period, so the cross-validation is not independent of the test set; it checks whether the ranking holds when the forecast origin moves.

```{r}
#| label: cv
#| cache: true

reg_pdq <- fit_reg$Reg[[1]]$fit$spec
cv_origins <- 13
cv_h       <- 12

cv_data <- nights_sold |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = nrow(train), .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id <= cv_origins)

cv_fc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(cv_origins), function(i) {
  d   <- cv_data |> filter(.id == i) |> select(-.id)
  fut <- new_data(d, cv_h)

  # seasonal naive and Project 1 SARIMA
  dB <- d |> mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
  f1 <- forecast(d  |> model(`Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(nights)), h = cv_h)
  f2 <- forecast(dB |> model(`SARIMA (Project 1)` =
                               ARIMA(log(nights) ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))), h = cv_h)

  # regression with ARIMA errors (orders fixed)
  dR <- covid_vars(d, delta_hat)
  fR <- covid_vars(fut, delta_hat)
  f3 <- forecast(dR |> model(Reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                                           pdq(reg_pdq$p, 1, reg_pdq$q) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))),
                 new_data = fR)

  # exponential smoothing on the imputed series
  dI <- impute_covid(d) |> as_tsibble(index = Month)
  f4 <- forecast(dI |> model(
    `ETS(A,N,A)`   = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`    = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))),
    h = cv_h)

  bind_rows(as_tibble(f1), as_tibble(f2), as_tibble(f3), as_tibble(f4)) |>
    select(.model, Month, .mean) |>
    group_by(.model) |>
    mutate(h = row_number(), origin = i) |>
    ungroup()
})) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(nights_sold) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  filter(!is.na(actual))

cv_by_h <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(.model, h) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2)), .groups = "drop")

cv_overall <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(Model = .model) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2)),
            MAE  = mean(abs(actual - .mean)),
            MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - .mean) / actual),
            n    = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(RMSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cv
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling-origin cross-validation (13 origins, horizons 1 to 12 months), averaged over all origins and horizons that fall inside the observed data. RMSE and MAE in thousands of nights."

cv_overall |> kable(digits = c(0, 1, 1, 2, 0))
cv_best <- cv_overall$Model[1]
cvr <- function(m) cv_overall$RMSE[cv_overall$Model == m]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv
#| fig-cap: "Rolling-origin cross-validation RMSE by forecast horizon."
#| fig-height: 3.5

ggplot(cv_by_h, aes(h, RMSE, colour = .model)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Forecast horizon (months)", y = "RMSE (thousands)", colour = NULL)
```

## Results

**Overall ranking.** On the test set the lowest RMSE is achieved by the **`r best_all`** model (`r fmt(rg(best_all, "RMSE"))` thousand nights). Among the models that passed the diagnostic step, the best is **`r best_cand`**. For reference, the Project 1 SARIMA has an RMSE of `r fmt(rg("SARIMA (Project 1)", "RMSE"))` and the seasonal naive benchmark `r fmt(rg("Seasonal naive", "RMSE"))`. In cross-validation the best model is **`r cv_best`** (RMSE `r fmt(cvr(cv_best))`)`r if (cv_best != "SARIMA (Project 1)") paste0(", against ", fmt(cvr("SARIMA (Project 1)")), " for the Project 1 SARIMA") else paste0(", followed by ", cv_overall$Model[2], " (", fmt(cv_overall$RMSE[2]), ")")`, with seasonal naive at `r fmt(cvr("Seasonal naive"))` (@tbl-cv, @fig-cv). The two evaluations therefore do not fully agree, which is exactly why a single test set is not enough: the cross-validation forecasts start later (up to June 2025) and are at most 12 months ahead, so they reward models that track the recent level and penalise less for how the trend is extrapolated in the second year.

**Static regression.** The static regression has an RMSE of `r fmt(rg("Static regression", "RMSE"))`, `r if (beats_sn("Static regression")) "beating seasonal naive despite its autocorrelated errors" else "worse than seasonal naive"`. Its deterministic trend is estimated from the whole training period, including the gentle decline before 2020, and is extrapolated through the test period, so the forecasts drift away from the data. Its 95% intervals happen to cover `r pct(rg("Static regression", "cover95"))` of the test months, but only because the COVID months inflate the residual variance; with autocorrelated errors the interval formula itself is not valid, so this coverage cannot be relied on.

**Regression with ARIMA errors.** Modelling the error process gives an RMSE of `r fmt(rg("Reg", "RMSE"))` and a MAPE of `r fmt(rg("Reg", "MAPE"), 2)`%, `r if (rg("Reg", "RMSE") < rg("SARIMA (Project 1)", "RMSE")) "better than" else "slightly worse than"` the Project 1 SARIMA. Its intervals cover `r pct(rg("Reg", "cover95"))` of the test months at the 95% level and `r pct(rg("Reg", "cover80"))` at the 80% level, so they are too wide: a correct 80% interval should miss about one month in five. The reason is visible in @fig-reg-resid. The intervention terms capture the collapse but not every month of the uneven recovery, so the innovations in 2020 and 2021 are several times larger than normal and inflate the estimated error variance, which then widens every forecast interval (mean width `r fmt(rg("Reg", "width95"), 0)` thousand nights against `r fmt(rg("SARIMA (Project 1)", "width95"), 0)` for the SARIMA, which ignores those months). By June 2024 the temporary part of the shock had died out ($\hat\delta^{\,50} \approx$ `r formatC(delta_hat^50, format = "e", digits = 1)`), so the forecasts rest on the post-COVID level and the seasonal dummies. The main advantage of this model is *interpretation*: it estimates the size, shape and persistence of the shock (@fig-intervention) instead of discarding it.

**Exponential smoothing on the raw data.** ETS fitted with the COVID months included reaches an RMSE of `r fmt(rg("ETS raw (original scale)", "RMSE"))`, `r if (beats_sn("ETS raw (original scale)")) "only just beating" else "not beating"` seasonal naive. With $\hat\alpha = 1$ it is close to a seasonal random walk, and its 95% intervals are on average `r fmt(rg("ETS raw (original scale)", "width95"), 0)` thousand nights wide, against `r fmt(rg("Reg", "width95"), 0)` for the regression.

**Exponential smoothing on the imputed series.** Imputing the window transforms exponential smoothing. The best of the seasonal models on the test set is **`r best_ets`** (RMSE `r fmt(rg(best_ets, "RMSE"))`), and the ranking among them is decided by the trend: the undamped Holt–Winters model (RMSE `r fmt(rg("Holt-Winters", "RMSE"))`) extrapolates a fixed negative slope for two years, the no-trend model (RMSE `r fmt(rg("ETS(A,N,A)", "RMSE"))`) holds the level flat, and the damped model (RMSE `r fmt(rg("Damped HW", "RMSE"))`) lets the slope fade. `r if (best_aicc != best_ets) paste0("AICc preferred ", best_aicc, ", which is a useful reminder that AICc measures one-step-ahead fit in the training data, while the test set measures forecasts up to 24 months ahead, where the treatment of the trend dominates.") else "Here AICc and the test set agree."` The undamped model's intervals also cover only `r pct(rg("Holt-Winters", "cover95"))` of the test months at the 95% level: its forecasts drift away from the data while the intervals stay narrow, partly because the noise-free imputed months shrink the estimated error variance. SES, which ignores the season, is far behind (RMSE `r fmt(rg("SES", "RMSE"))`), confirming the diagnostics.

# Comparison with Project 1

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-cap: "How the COVID-19 break is handled across Projects 1 and 3, with test set RMSE (thousands of nights) on the same July 2024 to June 2026 test set. The COVID-kept SARIMA result is taken from the Project 1 report."

tibble(
  `Treatment of the COVID months` = c(
    "Kept, no special treatment (Project 1, Design A)",
    "Kept, level resets each month (ETS raw)",
    "Treated as missing (Project 1, Design B)",
    "Modelled with intervention terms (regression with ARIMA errors)",
    paste0("Imputed by regression, then exponential smoothing (", best_ets, ")")
  ),
  Model = c("SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)", "ETS", "SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)", "Reg", best_ets),
  `Test RMSE` = c("3,243.5 (from Project 1)",
                  fmt(c(rg("ETS raw (original scale)", "RMSE"),
                        rg("SARIMA (Project 1)", "RMSE"),
                        rg("Reg", "RMSE"), rg(best_ets, "RMSE"))))
) |>
  kable()
```

Across the two projects the same series has now been forecast with five treatments of the structural break (@tbl-compare). The main lesson is that *any* sensible treatment of the break (deleting the months, modelling them, or imputing them) does far better than ignoring it in a model that assumes constant parameters. Between the sensible treatments, the differences in what each model *tells* us are larger than the differences in accuracy: only the regression quantifies the shock, while the imputation route lets a simple, transparent method (exponential smoothing) be used at all. Project 4 takes the remaining route: a state space model that treats the COVID months as missing without imputing anything.

# Discussion

## Key findings {#sec-findings}

1. **A static regression is not enough.** Trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms give an adjusted $R^2$ of `r fmt(static_glance$adj_r_squared, 3)`, but the residuals are strongly autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson `r fmt(dw_static, 2)`), so the standard errors and intervals cannot be trusted. Its test RMSE was `r fmt(rg("Static regression", "RMSE"))`.
2. **Regression with ARIMA errors fixes this.** With deterministic seasonal dummies (preferred to Fourier terms by AICc), a decaying intervention with $\hat\delta$ = `r fmt(delta_hat, 2)` (half-life about `r fmt(log(0.5) / log(delta_hat), 1)` months), two pulses and a level shift, the innovations are white noise (Ljung and Box p = `r pfmt(lbp("Reg"))`), and the test RMSE is `r fmt(rg("Reg", "RMSE"))` against `r fmt(rg("SARIMA (Project 1)", "RMSE"))` for the Project 1 SARIMA. The shock is described with five parameters instead of 25 deleted months. The post-COVID level is estimated (by the imputation regression) to be `r pct(1 - exp(imp_ramp), 0)` below the pre-COVID path.
3. **Exponential smoothing breaks on the raw data.** With the COVID months included, the level smoothing parameter goes to 1 and, on the log scale, AICc even drops the seasonal component.
4. **Regression imputation rescues exponential smoothing.** On the imputed series the seasonal models pass the diagnostics, and `r best_ets` reached a test RMSE of `r fmt(rg(best_ets, "RMSE"))`. The trend assumption (none, linear or damped) is what separates the seasonal models over a two-year horizon.
5. **My own Holt–Winters code reproduces `ETS()`.** The SSE agrees to `r fmt(abs(own_opt$value - fable_sse) / fable_sse * 100, 2)`% and both put $\beta$ and $\gamma$ at the boundary, confirming a fixed seasonal pattern and slope.
6. **Using only the post-COVID years** (@sec-post) avoids imputation, but leaves just `r nrow(train_post)` months. The best exponential smoothing model fitted to that window was `r best_post` (test RMSE `r fmt(pa(best_post, d_post, "RMSE"))`), against `r fmt(pa("Damped HW", d_imp, "RMSE"))` for damped Holt–Winters on the imputed series. `r post_rng <- range(post_acc$RMSE[post_acc$Data == d_post]); if (diff(post_rng) > 20) paste0('Across the three trend forms the post-COVID RMSE ranged from ', fmt(post_rng[1]), ' to ', fmt(post_rng[2]), ', so with so little data the result depends heavily on the choice of trend.') else 'The three trend forms gave similar results on this window.'` The damped model was the only one whose accuracy barely changed between the two training windows, which makes it the most robust choice.
7. **Overall,** the best model on the test set was `r best_all`, the best that also passed the diagnostics was `r best_cand`, and the best in cross-validation was `r cv_best`. `r if (cv_best == "SARIMA (Project 1)") paste0("Among the Section 2 models, ", cv_overall$Model[cv_overall$Model != "SARIMA (Project 1)"][1], " was the most accurate in cross-validation, so the Project 1 SARIMA remains a very strong benchmark: regression and exponential smoothing match it, but only beat it clearly on one of the two evaluations.") else ""`

## Issues and limitations

* **The imputed values are treated as data.** Exponential smoothing sees the 25 imputed months as exact observations with no noise. This makes the estimated error variance too small (so the intervals are too narrow) and can pull the smoothing parameters, since the imputed stretch is perfectly smooth. Multiple imputation (adding resampled residuals to the imputed values and averaging over many fits) would address this.
* **The imputation model is a modelling choice.** The linear ramp between the pre- and post-COVID levels is a simple assumption. A different path (for example a faster or slower recovery) would change the imputed level in 2021 and, through the smoothing, the estimated slope.
* **Choice of intervention shape.** The decay, pulses and step were chosen by looking at the data, so there is a risk of over-fitting the shape of the shock to this series. The pulse months were picked by eye.
* **Profile likelihood standard errors.** Treating $\hat\delta$ as known when computing the other standard errors understates their uncertainty.
* **Cross-validation shortcuts.** The regression's $\delta$ and error orders, and the ETS forms, were held fixed across origins, which favours them slightly because they were chosen with the full training set.

## What I would do differently

I would use multiple imputation for the COVID window so that the exponential smoothing intervals reflect the uncertainty in the imputed values, and estimate $\delta$ jointly with the other regression parameters by maximising the likelihood directly. A cleaner solution to both problems is a model that can skip the missing months without imputing them and that has the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is what the state space models in Project 4 provide.

## Reflection and model development

Project 1 left me with one clear problem: the COVID collapse was the biggest obstacle to forecasting accommodation demand, and the best I could do with SARIMA was to treat those 25 months as missing. That felt unsatisfying, because those months contain real information about how demand behaves under a shock. Section 2 of the course introduced two approaches that handle this very differently, time series regression and exponential smoothing, so I wanted to see whether *modelling* the shock, rather than deleting it, would give better forecasts or at least a better understanding of what happened.

The project changed shape considerably along the way. My first versions were framed around "modelling the COVID shock" and combined a single ETS model, a regression with intervention terms and a basic structural model fitted with the Kalman filter. As the portfolio came together, I realised this mixed topics from different parts of the course, and that the state space material belonged in Project 4, where it could be developed properly. I refocused this project on regression and exponential smoothing alone, which gave me room to go much deeper into each one. It also let me address a weakness I had listed in my own earlier draft, that everything rested on a single test set, by adding rolling-origin cross-validation.

On the regression side, I deliberately started with the simplest possible model, a static regression with a trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms. Its adjusted $R^2$ of 0.965 looked excellent, but the residuals drifted in long runs and the Durbin–Watson statistic was 0.53. That was the moment the lectures' warning about regression on time series became concrete for me: a good in-sample fit can hide errors that make every standard error and interval unreliable. Letting the errors follow an ARIMA process fixed this, and each remaining decision came from the data. I replaced the deterministic trend with a first difference because the post-COVID level clearly did not follow a straight line. I kept seasonal dummies rather than Fourier terms because the sharp December peak needs many harmonics, which AICc confirmed. And because the decay rate enters the model non-linearly, I chose it by profiling the AICc over a grid. The most subtle lesson was in interpreting the result. With a unit root in the errors, the level shift coefficient is not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels, because part of the recovery is carried by the error process. I only understood this properly once the imputation regression gave a very different estimate of that gap.

Exponential smoothing taught me the opposite lesson about COVID. Fitted to the raw data, the level smoothing parameter went straight to 1, and on the log scale the model even dropped the seasonal component altogether. Unlike ARIMA, exponential smoothing cannot skip missing months, so I had to decide what to put in the gap. I chose to impute the window with a regression fitted only to the non-COVID months, which carries the seasonal pattern across the gap with a smooth transition between the two levels. Writing the Holt–Winters recursions myself was the most useful part of this section. It reproduced `ETS()` almost exactly, and it showed me something I would have missed by only calling the function: the 13 initial states are parameters too, and they dominate the estimation.

The results did not always agree with each other, and working out why was the most valuable part of the project. AICc preferred the undamped Holt–Winters model, but on the test set it was one of the worst, because it extrapolated a fixed downward slope for two full years, while the damped version, which lets the slope fade, was the best model of all. The test set and the cross-validation also disagreed: damped Holt–Winters won on the test set, but the Project 1 SARIMA won in cross-validation. This showed me that in-sample criteria measure one-step fit, while forecasting over two years depends mostly on how the trend is extrapolated, and that a single test set is not enough to rank models.

I also tested an idea of my own. Since exponential smoothing already puts most of its weight on recent observations, I wondered whether the imputation was needed at all, or whether I could simply fit the models to the post-COVID years from April 2022. Working through it showed me that the weighting only applies to the level: in my models the seasonal pattern and the slope barely update, so they still come from the start of the series in 2015. Fitting only the last two years was the way to let them reflect current behaviour, at the cost of having just 27 months of data. The results were mixed. The undamped Holt–Winters model improved a great deal, because it no longer extrapolated a slope from 2015, but the no-trend model got worse. The damped model gave almost the same accuracy on both windows, which convinced me more than any single score that damping is the safest choice when the trend is uncertain. The seasonal pattern learned from two years was also very close to the one from the full series, which confirmed again how stable it is. In the end I kept the imputed series as the main approach, because with so little data the outcome depended too much on which trend I happened to choose.

Going forward, the main weakness I would address is that the imputed COVID months are treated as exact data. They contain no noise, which makes the exponential smoothing intervals too narrow; multiple imputation would fix this. More fundamentally, both approaches in this project needed a workaround for the missing months, either intervention terms or imputation. A state space model can skip missing observations directly while keeping the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is exactly what Project 4 takes up.
